events.title: The Guardian reveals bulk collection of Verizon call records, then PRISM
events.summary: On 5 June 2013 The Guardian published a top-secret Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court order, granted on 25 April, requiring Verizon to hand the NSA call records 'on an ongoing, daily basis', including domestic calls. A second story reported an NSA programme called PRISM, described in a 41-slide training presentation, that collected search history, email content, file transfers and live chats from Google, Facebook, Apple and other US internet companies; the companies denied knowledge of it. The US Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board later dated the first story to 5 June 2013 and described it as the first of a series based on documents disclosed by Edward Snowden.
events.significance: Showed that privacy's walls had moved inside the phone network and the cloud, where people could neither see nor object to collection — the grievance that later drove Schrems, the GDPR's enforcement and demands for user-side controls.

sources.institution: The Guardian
sources.title: NSA collecting phone records of millions of Verizon customers daily
sources.quote: The order, a copy of which has been obtained by the Guardian, requires Verizon on an "ongoing, daily basis" to give the NSA information on all telephone calls in its systems , both within the US and between the US and other countries.
sources.note: The page now shows a timestamp of Thu 6 June 2013 06.05 EDT (a later update); the story first appeared on the evening of 5 June US time. The space before the comma is in the page text.

sources.institution: Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board (US)
sources.title: Report on the Telephone Records Program Conducted under Section 215 of the USA PATRIOT Act and on the Operations of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court
sources.quote: On June 5, 2013, the British newspaper The Guardian published the first of a series of articles based on unauthorized disclosures of classified documents by Edward Snowden, a contractor for the National Security Agency (“NSA”).

sources.institution: The Guardian
sources.title: NSA Prism program taps in to user data of Apple, Google and others
sources.quote: The NSA access is part of a previously undisclosed program called Prism , which allows officials to collect material including search history, the content of emails, file transfers and live chats, the document says.
sources.note: URL dated 6 June 2013; the page timestamp (7 June 2013 15.23 EDT) reflects a later update.

events.locationNote: The Guardian's London headquarters at Kings Place; the Verizon story was reported by Glenn Greenwald from Hong Kong and edited in London and New York.

events.title: Edward Snowden identifies himself as the source, from Hong Kong
events.summary: On 9 June 2013 The Guardian named its source, at his request, as Edward Snowden, a 29-year-old former CIA technical assistant then employed by the contractor Booz Allen Hamilton, who had worked at the NSA for four years through outside contractors. He had flown to Hong Kong on 20 May.
events.significance: Put a human face on the gap between what people had agreed to and what was being done with their data, making surveillance a mass public issue across the democracies.

sources.institution: The Guardian
sources.title: Edward Snowden: the whistleblower behind the NSA surveillance revelations
sources.quote: Edward Snowden , a 29-year-old former technical assistant for the CIA and current employee of the defence contractor Booz Allen Hamilton. Snowden has been working at the National Security Agency for the last four years as an employee of various outside contractors, including Booz Allen and Dell.
sources.note: The space before the comma is in the page text. Same article: 'The Guardian, after several days of interviews, is revealing his identity at his request.' and 'On May 20, he boarded a flight to Hong Kong, where he has remained ever since.'

sources.institution: The Guardian
sources.title: Edward Snowden: the whistleblower behind the NSA surveillance revelations
sources.quote: On May 20, he boarded a flight to Hong Kong, where he has remained ever since.

events.locationNote: City-level coordinates (Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon), where Snowden met the journalists; the exact hotel is not cited here.

events.title: EU Court of Justice: search engines must delist on request (Google Spain)
events.place: Court of Justice of the European Union, Kirchberg, Luxembourg
events.summary: In Case C-131/12, brought after Mario Costeja González complained in 2010 to Spain's data protection agency about search results linking to 1998 La Vanguardia pages announcing a real-estate auction, the Grand Chamber held that a search engine operator processes personal data and can be obliged to remove links to lawful third-party pages from results for a person's name. It held that the data subject's rights under Articles 7 and 8 of the Charter override, as a rule, both the operator's economic interest and the public's interest in finding the information, unless the person's role in public life justifies access.
events.significance: Established that an individual can make a claim directly against a global platform about how information on them is surfaced — a person-initiated request with legal force, the first widely used 'right to be forgotten'.

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union (Grand Chamber), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Judgment of the Court (Grand Chamber) of 13 May 2014, Google Spain SL and Google Inc. v Agencia Española de Protección de Datos (AEPD) and Mario Costeja González, Case C-131/12, EU:C:2014:317
sources.quote: As the data subject may, in the light of his fundamental rights under Articles 7 and 8 of the Charter, request that the information in question no longer be made available to the general public by its inclusion in such a list of results, it should be held, as follows in particular from paragraph 81 of the present judgment, that those rights override, as a rule, not only the economic interest of the operator of the search engine but also the interest of the general public in finding that information upon a search relating to the data subject’s name.
sources.note: Paragraph 97. curia.europa.eu's judgment viewer blocks scripted access; the identical official text is served by the EU Publications Office repository (CELEX 62012CJ0131).

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union
sources.title: Press Release No 70/14: Judgment in Case C-131/12 Google Spain SL, Google Inc. v Agencia Española de Protección de Datos, Mario Costeja González
sources.quote: In 2010 Mario Costeja González, a Spanish national, lodged with the Agencia Española de Protección de Datos (Spanish Data Protection Agency, the AEPD) a complaint against La Vanguardia Ediciones SL (the publisher of a daily newspaper with a large circulation in Spain, in particular in Catalonia) and against Google Spain and Google Inc.

events.locationNote: Seat of the Court of Justice, Luxembourg.

events.title: Schrems I: the EU Court of Justice strikes down Safe Harbour
events.place: Court of Justice of the European Union, Kirchberg, Luxembourg
events.summary: Maximillian Schrems, an Austrian Facebook user since 2008, complained to the Irish Data Protection Commissioner that, in light of Snowden's 2013 revelations, US law did not protect data transferred there from surveillance. In Case C-362/14 the Grand Chamber declared the Commission's 2000 Safe Harbour decision (2000/520) invalid, holding that laws allowing public authorities generalised access to the content of electronic communications compromise the essence of the right to private life.
events.significance: One individual's complaint dismantled the legal basis for transatlantic data flows, proving that a person could force the system to answer for where their data goes.

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union (Grand Chamber), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Judgment of the Court (Grand Chamber) of 6 October 2015, Maximillian Schrems v Data Protection Commissioner, Case C-362/14, EU:C:2015:650
sources.quote: In particular, legislation permitting the public authorities to have access on a generalised basis to the content of electronic communications must be regarded as compromising the essence of the fundamental right to respect for private life, as guaranteed by Article 7 of the Charter
sources.note: Paragraph 94. Operative part: 'Decision 2000/520 is invalid.' Official text via the EU Publications Office repository (CELEX 62014CJ0362).

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union
sources.title: Press Release No 117/15: The Court of Justice declares that the Commission's US Safe Harbour Decision is invalid
sources.quote: Maximillian Schrems, an Austrian citizen, has been a Facebook user since 2008.

events.locationNote: Seat of the Court of Justice, Luxembourg.

events.title: The GDPR is signed — with a right to object 'by automated means'
events.summary: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the General Data Protection Regulation, was signed at Brussels on 27 April 2016 and published in the Official Journal on 4 May 2016, to apply from 25 May 2018. Article 21(5) lets a person exercise the right to object to processing, in the context of information society services, 'by automated means using technical specifications'. Article 25 requires data protection by design and by default, so that by default only the personal data necessary for each specific purpose are processed.
events.significance: Article 21(5) is the first clause in a major privacy law that anticipates a person's software stating their objection for them — the legal hook on which machine-readable signals such as Global Privacy Control and person-proffered terms can hang.

sources.institution: European Parliament and Council of the European Union (Official Journal L 119, 4.5.2016), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation), Article 21(5)
sources.quote: In the context of the use of information society services, and notwithstanding Directive 2002/58/EC, the data subject may exercise his or her right to object by automated means using technical specifications.
sources.note: EUR-Lex (eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj) blocks scripted access; the identical Official Journal text (CELEX 32016R0679) was read from the EU Publications Office repository.

sources.institution: European Parliament and Council of the European Union (Official Journal L 119, 4.5.2016), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 25(2) — Data protection by design and by default
sources.quote: The controller shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures for ensuring that, by default, only personal data which are necessary for each specific purpose of the processing are processed.

sources.institution: European Parliament and Council of the European Union (Official Journal L 119, 4.5.2016), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 99(2) and signature
sources.quote: It shall apply from 25 May 2018.
sources.note: The act closes 'Done at Brussels, 27 April 2016.' The Official Journal header dates publication 4.5.2016.

events.locationNote: The regulation was signed at Brussels; coordinates are the European Parliament's Brussels seat. The Parliament's final plenary vote took place in Strasbourg.

events.title: The European Commission adopts the EU-US Privacy Shield
events.summary: Nine months after Safe Harbour fell, the Commission adopted Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/1250, finding that the United States ensured an adequate level of protection for personal data transferred to organisations that self-certified under a new EU-US Privacy Shield. The Court of Justice invalidated this decision four years later in Schrems II.
events.significance: A replacement negotiated between governments, not with the people whose data moved — and it did not survive judicial review.

sources.institution: European Commission (Official Journal of the European Union L 207, 1.8.2016), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/1250 of 12 July 2016 on the adequacy of the protection provided by the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield
sources.quote: Based on the findings developed in recitals 136-140, the Commission concludes that the United States ensures an adequate level of protection for personal data transferred under the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield from the Union to self-certified organisations in the United States.
sources.note: Recital 141; signed 'Done at Brussels, 12 July 2016.' Official text via the EU Publications Office repository (CELEX 32016D1250).

events.title: India's Supreme Court declares privacy a fundamental right
events.place: Supreme Court of India, Tilak Marg, New Delhi
events.summary: In Justice K S Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India, a challenge arising from the Aadhaar biometric identity programme, a nine-judge bench unanimously overruled M P Sharma and, in part, Kharak Singh and held that privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21. The lead opinion by Justice D Y Chandrachud recognised informational privacy, warned that threats come from non-state actors as well as the state, and urged the government to put in place a robust data protection regime.
events.significance: Extended constitutional privacy to the world's most populous democracy — and explicitly to threats from private, non-state actors holding data, not only the state.

sources.institution: Supreme Court of India
sources.title: Justice K S Puttaswamy (Retd.) and Anr. v Union of India and Ors., Writ Petition (Civil) No 494 of 2012 — Order of the Court
sources.quote: (iii) The right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution.
sources.note: Order of the Court signed by all nine judges, 'New Delhi; AUGUST 24, 2017' (final pages of the 547-page PDF).

sources.institution: Supreme Court of India
sources.title: Justice K S Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India — judgment of Dr D Y Chandrachud J (for Khehar CJI, Agrawal, Nazeer JJ and himself)
sources.quote: Informational privacy is a facet of the right to privacy. The dangers to privacy in an age of information can originate not only from the state but from non-state actors as well.
sources.note: Same judgment also reads: 'We commend to the Union Government the need to examine and put into place a robust regime for data protection.'

sources.institution: Supreme Court of India
sources.title: Justice K S Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India — judgment of Dr D Y Chandrachud J
sources.quote: It arises in the context of a constitutional challenge to the Aadhaar project, which aims to build a database of personal identity and biometric information covering every Indian – the world’s largest endeavour of its kind.

events.title: Equifax discloses a breach eventually counted at 147 million people
events.summary: On 7 September 2017 the credit bureau Equifax announced that criminals had exploited a website application vulnerability between mid-May and July 2017, initially estimating that about 143 million US consumers were affected; names, Social Security numbers, birth dates and addresses were taken. On 22 July 2019 the FTC announced a global settlement with the FTC, the CFPB and 50 US states and territories of at least $575 million and potentially up to $700 million, putting the number affected at approximately 147 million.
events.significance: People whose data was taken had never chosen to deal with Equifax at all — a stark case of data held about people without any relationship or terms of their own.

sources.institution: US Federal Trade Commission
sources.title: Equifax to Pay $575 Million as Part of Settlement with FTC, CFPB, and States Related to 2017 Data Breach
sources.quote: Equifax Inc. has agreed to pay at least $575 million, and potentially up to $700 million, as part of a global settlement with the Federal Trade Commission, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), and 50 U.S. states and territories, which alleged that the credit reporting company’s failure to take reasonable steps to secure its network led to a data breach in 2017 that affected approximately 147 million people.

sources.institution: Equifax Inc. (investor relations, via PR Newswire)
sources.title: Equifax Announces Cybersecurity Incident Involving Consumer Information
sources.quote: Equifax Inc. (NYSE: EFX) today announced a cybersecurity incident potentially impacting approximately 143 million U.S. consumers. Criminals exploited a U.S. website application vulnerability to gain access to certain files. Based on the company's investigation, the unauthorized access occurred from mid-May through July 2017.
sources.note: The initial estimate (143 million) was later revised upward; the FTC settlement uses approximately 147 million.

events.locationNote: Equifax corporate headquarters, 1550 Peachtree Street NW, Atlanta, Georgia.

events.title: Cambridge Analytica: Facebook data of up to 87 million people
events.place: The Observer / The Guardian, Kings Place, London
events.summary: On 17 March 2018 The Observer reported that the political consultancy Cambridge Analytica, which had worked with Donald Trump's election team, had harvested millions of Facebook profiles of US voters to build software to predict and influence voting choices. The data came through a personality-quiz app, 'thisisyourdigitallife', built by the researcher Aleksandr Kogan; about 270,000 people downloaded it, but it also collected information about their friends. On 4 April 2018 Facebook estimated that the information of up to 87 million people, mostly in the US, may have been improperly shared.
events.significance: Showed that one person's 'consent' on a platform could hand over the data of friends who had agreed to nothing — the clearest demonstration that platform-defined consent does not express individual intent.

sources.institution: The Guardian / The Observer
sources.title: Revealed: 50 million Facebook profiles harvested for Cambridge Analytica in major data breach
sources.quote: The data analytics firm that worked with Donald Trump’s election team and the winning Brexit campaign harvested millions of Facebook profiles of US voters, in one of the tech giant’s biggest ever data breaches, and used them to build a powerful software program to predict and influence choices at the ballot box.
sources.note: The Observer's initial estimate was 50 million profiles; Facebook's later estimate was up to 87 million.

sources.institution: Facebook (Meta) Newsroom
sources.title: An Update on Our Plans to Restrict Data Access on Facebook (Mike Schroepfer)
sources.quote: In total, we believe the Facebook information of up to 87 million people — mostly in the US — may have been improperly shared with Cambridge Analytica.

sources.institution: Facebook (Meta) Newsroom
sources.title: Suspending Cambridge Analytica and SCL Group From Facebook (Paul Grewal)
sources.quote: Approximately 270,000 people downloaded the app. In so doing, they gave their consent for Kogan to access information such as the city they set on their profile, or content they had liked, as well as more limited information about friends who had their privacy settings set to allow it.
sources.note: Company statement, cited for Facebook's own account of the app. Updated 17 March 2018 to say 'The claim that this is a data breach is completely false.'

events.locationNote: The Observer's newsroom at Kings Place, London (shared with The Guardian).

events.title: The GDPR applies — and the consent pop-ups multiply
events.summary: From 25 May 2018 the GDPR applied across the EU. Consent had to be as easy to withdraw as to give (Article 7(3)), and the most serious infringements became punishable by fines of up to €20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (Article 83(5)). On the first day, Max Schrems's new organisation noyb filed four complaints against Google (Android), Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram over 'forced consent', as 'consent boxes' popped up across the web.
events.significance: Turned privacy from a promise into a liability on the balance sheet — but its most visible product was the consent banner, in which the site, not the person, sets the terms and the choices.

sources.institution: European Parliament and Council of the European Union (Official Journal L 119, 4.5.2016), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 83(5) — General conditions for imposing administrative fines
sources.quote: Infringements of the following provisions shall, in accordance with paragraph 2, be subject to administrative fines up to 20 000 000 EUR, or in the case of an undertaking, up to 4 % of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher

sources.institution: European Parliament and Council of the European Union (Official Journal L 119, 4.5.2016), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 7(3) — Conditions for consent
sources.quote: The data subject shall have the right to withdraw his or her consent at any time. The withdrawal of consent shall not affect the lawfulness of processing based on consent before its withdrawal. Prior to giving consent, the data subject shall be informed thereof. It shall be as easy to withdraw as to give consent.

sources.institution: noyb – European Center for Digital Rights
sources.title: noyb.eu filed complaints over “forced consent” against Google, Instagram, WhatsApp and Facebook
sources.quote: The opposite feeling spread on the screens of many users: tons of “consent boxes” popped up online or in applications, often combined with a threat that the service can no longer be used if users do not consent. On the first day of GDPR noyb.eu has therefore filed four complaints against Google (Android), Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram over “forced consent”.
sources.note: noyb is an advocacy organisation; cited for what it itself did. The complaints went to the French, Belgian, Hamburg and Austrian authorities.

events.locationNote: The regulation applied simultaneously in every member state; coordinates are the European Commission in Brussels.

events.title: FTC imposes a $5 billion penalty on Facebook
events.place: Federal Trade Commission, 600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: The FTC announced that Facebook would pay a $5 billion penalty and accept new restrictions and a modified corporate structure to settle charges that it violated a 2012 FTC order by deceiving users about their ability to control the privacy of their information — including by sharing friends' data with third-party app developers even when those friends had set more restrictive settings. The same day the FTC announced actions against Cambridge Analytica, its former CEO Alexander Nix and the app developer Aleksandr Kogan.
events.significance: The US regulator's largest privacy penalty turned on a simple failure: the company undermined the preferences users had set — the problem that person-set, machine-readable terms are designed to make enforceable.

sources.institution: US Federal Trade Commission
sources.title: FTC Imposes $5 Billion Penalty and Sweeping New Privacy Restrictions on Facebook
sources.quote: Facebook, Inc. will pay a record-breaking $5 billion penalty, and submit to new restrictions and a modified corporate structure that will hold the company accountable for the decisions it makes about its users’ privacy, to settle Federal Trade Commission charges that the company violated a 2012 FTC order by deceiving users about their ability to control the privacy of their personal information.

sources.institution: US Federal Trade Commission
sources.title: FTC Imposes $5 Billion Penalty and Sweeping New Privacy Restrictions on Facebook
sources.quote: The FTC alleges that Facebook violated the 2012 order by deceiving its users when the company shared the data of users’ Facebook friends with third-party app developers, even when those friends had set more restrictive privacy settings.

events.locationNote: FTC headquarters, Washington, D.C., where the settlement was announced at a press conference.

events.title: Schrems II: the Court of Justice invalidates Privacy Shield
events.place: Court of Justice of the European Union, Kirchberg, Luxembourg
events.summary: On a reference from the Irish High Court in Case C-311/18, the Grand Chamber declared Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/1250 on the EU-US Privacy Shield invalid, while holding that the Commission's standard contractual clauses (Decision 2010/87) remained valid. It was Schrems's second successful challenge to the legal basis of EU-US data transfers.
events.significance: Confirmed that under the GDPR the individual's rights travel with the data, and that no political deal can override them without real redress.

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union (Grand Chamber), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Judgment of the Court (Grand Chamber) of 16 July 2020, Data Protection Commissioner v Facebook Ireland Ltd and Maximillian Schrems, Case C-311/18, EU:C:2020:559
sources.quote: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2016/1250 of 12 July 2016 pursuant to Directive 95/46/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council on the adequacy of the protection provided by the EU-US Privacy Shield is invalid.
sources.note: Operative part, point 5. Official text via the EU Publications Office repository (CELEX 62018CJ0311).

sources.institution: Court of Justice of the European Union
sources.title: Press Release No 91/20: The Court of Justice invalidates Decision 2016/1250 on the adequacy of the protection provided by the EU-US Data Protection Shield
sources.quote: However, it considers that Commission Decision 2010/87 on standard contractual clauses for the transfer of personal data to processors established in third countries is valid.

events.locationNote: Seat of the Court of Justice, Luxembourg (judgment delivered during COVID-19 restrictions).

events.title: Third attempt: the EU-US Data Privacy Framework
events.summary: After Schrems II, the United States adopted Executive Order 14086 on 7 October 2022, limiting signals-intelligence collection and creating a Data Protection Review Court. On 10 July 2023 the Commission adopted Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1795, finding that the United States ensures an adequate level of protection for data transferred to organisations certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework.
events.significance: The third transatlantic arrangement in eight years, it shows how contested the legal plumbing under every data flow remains — and why terms that travel with the person, not the pipe, are attractive.

sources.institution: European Commission (Official Journal of the European Union L 231, 20.9.2023), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1795 of 10 July 2023 on the adequate level of protection of personal data under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework
sources.quote: As a result of these discussions, the United States on 7 October 2022 adopted Executive Order 14086 ‘Enhancing Safeguards for US Signals Intelligence Activities’ (EO 14086), which is complemented by a Regulation on the Data Protection Review Court issued by the U.S. Attorney General (AG Regulation)
sources.note: Recital 6; signed 'Done at Brussels, 10 July 2023.' Official text via the EU Publications Office repository (CELEX 32023D1795).

sources.institution: European Commission (Official Journal of the European Union L 231, 20.9.2023), via EU Publications Office (Cellar)
sources.title: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1795 of 10 July 2023 — adequacy finding
sources.quote: Based on the findings set out in recitals 9-200, the Commission concludes that the United States ensures an adequate level of protection for personal data transferred under the EU-U.S. DPF from a controller or a processor in the Union
